title: std::chrono, std::filesystem, Ranges and Coroutines
objectives: Time code with steady_clock and convert durations explicitly with duration_cast, knowing which clock is trustworthy for what
Walk directories and query files portably with std::filesystem (C++17)
Read and write lazy Ranges pipelines (C++20) and state what they replace in C++17 code
Explain at survey level what coroutines (C++20) offer via co_yield and which library pieces arrive later (std::generator, C++23)
motivation: Latency is money: answering a fill a few hundred microseconds late bleeds edge on every message. But timing with the wall clock lies. NTP adjustments move it backwards mid-run, and filesystem code written per-platform rots. std::chrono gives durations and clocks whose behaviour is contractual, std::filesystem (C++17) makes data hygiene portable, and the C++20 additions. Ranges views and coroutines, reshape how streaming work is expressed. This lesson builds the measuring and data-walking toolkit, with every feature labelled by the standard it needs.

blocks.md: A **duration** is a count times a ratio: `std::chrono::nanoseconds`, `microseconds`, `milliseconds` - or your own `duration<double, std::ratio<1, 1000>>`. A **time_point** is a duration since an epoch, tied to a clock. The three standard clocks differ in what they guarantee, and choosing wrongly is the classic bug: `system_clock` is the wall clock, right for timestamps humans file, but NTP, DST and leap seconds move it, sometimes backwards. `steady_clock` is monotonic: it never jumps, so durations across it are trustworthy, it is *the* benchmarking clock. `high_resolution_clock` is an alias with no guarantees of being either; avoid it in production.

blocks.caption: Machine-dependent output by design, typical: about 1,000,000 ns total, roughly 1 ns per operation. Report the median of many runs, never one sample.

blocks.md: Durations do units-safe arithmetic: `t1 - t0` yields the clock's native duration, and `duration_cast<T>` converts with **truncation**, because 1500 ms is genuinely not two whole seconds. Literal suffixes such as `1500ms` or `2us` need `using namespace std::chrono_literals;` (C++14) and keep unit mistakes out of review. One discipline rule: stay in a single clock per measurement, converting between clock time points is where subtle off-by-a-leap-second bugs live.

blocks.caption: duration_cast truncates toward zero; the remainder stays in the finer unit.
A nanoseconds duration is one 64-bit signed count: headroom to time roughly 292 years without overflow, and every conversion is exact integer arithmetic on that count.

blocks.md: `std::filesystem` (C++17, `<filesystem>`) speaks paths, directories and files in one vocabulary across platforms: `fs::path` composes with `/`, `fs::directory_iterator` range-fors over a directory's entries, `recursive_directory_iterator` descends, and `exists`, `is_regular_file`, `file_size` answer metadata questions. The desk use is data hygiene, walk the tick archive, sum bytes per date file, catch stragglers before the backtest does. In latency-sensitive or racy paths, prefer the `error_code` overloads (`fs::file_size(p, ec)`) so a vanished file is a flag, not an exception.

blocks.caption: Output depends on the machine's data directory, the point is the vocabulary: iterate, filter, query, sum.

blocks.md: **Ranges (C++20)** turn algorithms into composable pipelines with the `|` pipe, and the critical property is laziness: `std::views::filter` and `std::views::transform` build **no new containers**, elements flow through the pipeline one at a time as the consumer iterates. One pass, zero intermediate allocation. The C++17 equivalent below is the same computation spelled with an explicit loop; views replace the loop-nesting or copy-into-temporary style, not the mathematics.

blocks.caption: Odds 3, 1, 1, 5, 9 give lots 300 + 100 + 100 + 500 + 900 = 1900.
Nothing executes until the for-loop iterates, then one element at a time.

blocks.md: **Coroutines (C++20)**: a function containing `co_await`, `co_yield` or `co_return` can suspend itself and resume later with all local state intact. `co_yield` turns a function into a **pull-based stream**, the consumer asks for the next tick, the coroutine runs until it has one, hands it over, and freezes in place. That maps naturally onto replaying tape captures or interleaving I/O with computation. Survey-level caveat with the standard label: C++20 ships the *language* machinery only; the standard `std::generator` type arrives with **C++23**, so C++20 code needs a hand-written promise type or a third-party library to get the `Generator` below.

blocks.caption: One tick materialised per pull: the pipeline never holds the whole tape in memory.

blocks.title: Timing lies you can avoid
blocks.md: Benchmarking with system_clock silently includes NTP steps; a single sample includes cold caches and page faults; and high_resolution_clock is an unspecified alias with no contract. The three-point discipline before quoting 'our latency is 620 ns': steady_clock, warm-up runs, median of many samples.

guidedExercise.prompt: You time a matching-engine pass with steady_clock: `t1 - t0` comes back as 6,200,000 nanoseconds over 1,000,000 price updates. (a) Convert the total to microseconds and to milliseconds. (b) Compute nanoseconds per update. (c) A colleague reports 6.2 ms for the same code using system_clock across a 10-minute run during which NTP stepped the clock back by 30 ms. Explain why that number can be wrong and what steady_clock's contract prevents.
hints: A monotonic clock never steps backwards or forwards: intervals across it are unaffected by what the wall clock did.
guidedExercise.solution:
(a) 6,200,000 ns $= 6{,}200$ microseconds $= 6.2$ ms.

(b) 6,200,000 ns over 1,000,000 updates $= \mathbf{6.2}$ **ns per update**.

(c) `system_clock` is the adjustable wall clock. If NTP steps it by 30 ms mid-run, any interval that spans the step is shifted by 30 ms: a 6.2 ms pass can be reported as roughly $-23.8$ ms (backwards step) or $+36.2$ ms (forward step), and the median of such samples is meaningless. `steady_clock` is monotonic **by contract**, it cannot step, so durations across it remain correct no matter what the wall clock does. Honest report: 6.2 ms per pass, median over many warm runs.

independentExercise.prompt: Size a tick-data archive: `data/ticks` contains ticks_0100.csv (4,000,000 bytes), ticks_0200.csv (2,500,000 bytes) and readme.md (1,750,000 bytes). (a) Write the C++17 filesystem loop that sums only .csv file sizes and state the exact total. (b) The scan takes 180 microseconds and directory iteration sees all 3 entries: express 180 us in nanoseconds and compute the per-entry cost. (c) Sketch the C++20 ranges pipeline that filters .csv entries and transforms them into sizes, labelling which parts are C++20-only.
hints: file_size returns std::uintmax_t, an unsigned byte count.
filter decides which entries pass; transform maps an entry to its size, both are views, both are C++20.

commonMistakes: Benchmarking with system_clock (steps with NTP) or high_resolution_clock (an unspecified alias), use steady_clock for all duration measurement.
Quoting a single timing sample: warm up first and report the median of many runs; means are dragged by outliers.
Forgetting duration_cast truncates: 1500 ms becomes 1 s plus a 500 ms remainder, not 1.5 in integer seconds.
Using throwing filesystem calls in latency-sensitive or racy paths: the error_code overloads make a vanished file a flag instead of an exception.
Expecting std::views pipelines to run eagerly: nothing happens until you iterate, and views, pipes and ranges are C++20, not C++17.
realWorldApplication: Every latency budget, soak test and benchmark harness is built on steady_clock and duration arithmetic, and filesystem walks power the data-integrity jobs behind any trading stack's archives.
quantFinanceApplication: A market-data replay engine streams a tape through a co_yield generator at research speed, while the live gateway budgets its 250 microseconds per order from steady_clock medians, the same toolkit, two sides of the latency line.
summary: Durations are count times ratio and clocks have contracts: steady_clock for timing (monotonic), system_clock for human wall timestamps.
duration_cast truncates and chrono literals (C++14) keep units readable; stay in one clock per measurement.
std::filesystem (C++17) gives portable paths, directory iteration and file queries, prefer error_code overloads in racy paths.
Ranges views (C++20) are lazy pipelines: filter and transform run one element at a time as the consumer iterates, with no intermediate containers.
Coroutines (C++20 language, std::generator C++23) express pull-based streaming via co_yield with full local state preserved across suspensions.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++17 program print?
quiz.explanation: duration_cast<seconds> truncates toward zero: 1500 ms is 1 whole second. The remainder stays expressible in the finer unit: ms, s is 500 milliseconds.

quiz.prompt: Which clock should you use to benchmark a hot loop, and why?
options: system_clock: it is the real wall time
steady_clock: monotonic, immune to NTP and DST adjustments
high_resolution_clock: it is the most precise by definition
Any clock: they are all equivalent for durations
quiz.explanation: steady_clock is contractually monotonic, it never steps, so intervals across it are trustworthy even when NTP moves the wall clock. high_resolution_clock is an unspecified alias, and system_clock is for human timestamps.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++17 program print?
quiz.explanation: The odd values are 3, 1, 1, 5, 9, the evens 4, 2, 6 are skipped, and 3+1+1+5+9 = 19. This is exactly the computation a C++20 filter view would express lazily.

quiz.prompt: A gateway spends 250 microseconds per order. Over 100,000 orders, how many seconds does it spend processing (give the value in seconds)?
quiz.explanation: 250 us x 100,000 = 25,000,000 us = 25 s. Unit conversions like this are exactly what chrono's duration types and duration_cast make hard to get wrong.

options: Ranges views and the | pipe. C++20
chrono literal suffixes such as 1500ms. C++14
quiz.explanation: std::generator is C++23: C++20 coroutines provide the language machinery (co_yield, co_await, co_return) but not a standard generator type. C++20 code needs a hand-written or third-party Generator.

quiz.prompt: (C++20) When does a std::views::filter / std::views::transform pipeline actually examine elements?
options: At construction: it copies matching elements immediately
Only as the consumer iterates, nothing runs until iteration, one element at a time
In a background thread the library spawns
At destruction of the view, in one batch
quiz.explanation: Views are lazy, non-owning adaptors: elements flow through the pipeline as the consumer iterates, which means one pass and zero intermediate containers.

flashcards.back: steady_clock: contractually monotonic, never adjusted. NTP/DST cannot move it, so durations are trustworthy. system_clock is for wall timestamps; high_resolution_clock is an unspecified alias.
